from PIL import Image
import numpy as np, colorsys
im = Image.open('barcode.png').convert('RGB')
a = np.asarray(im).astype(float)
h,w,_ = a.shape
sw=4; n=w//sw
cols=[]
for i in range(n):
    m = a[:, i*sw:(i+1)*sw, :].mean(axis=(0,1))
    hh,ss,vv = colorsys.rgb_to_hsv(*(m/255))
    cols.append((i/n*100, m, hh*360, ss, vv))

print()
# very bright stripes v>0.65
bright=[c for c in cols if c[4]>0.65]
print('bright stripes:')
for c in bright:
    print(f'{c[0]:.1f}%  RGB {tuple(round(x) for x in c[1])}')
"

2011 American film

Puncture

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/ae/Puncture_Poster.jpg/250px-Puncture_Poster.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Puncture_Poster.jpg) Theatrical release poster

***Puncture*** (released under the title ***Injustice*** in the United Kingdom) is an independent feature film starring [Chris Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Evans_\(actor\) "Chris Evans (actor)"), directed by [Adam Kassen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Kassen "Adam Kassen") and [Mark Kassen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Kassen "Mark Kassen"). The film is based on the true story of [Michael David "Mike" Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_David_Weiss "Michael David Weiss") and Paul Danziger. It was chosen as one of the spotlight films for the 2011 [Tribeca Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribeca_Film_Festival "Tribeca Film Festival"), premiering on April 21, 2011, in New York City.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Puncture_\(film\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

Mike Weiss, a young Houston lawyer and drug addict, and Paul Danziger, his longtime friend and straitlaced law partner, are the personal injury lawyers behind the law firm Danziger & Weiss. They decide to take on a case involving Vicky Rogers, a local ER nurse, who was [pricked by a contaminated needle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needlestick_injury "Needlestick injury") on the job and contracted HIV. Vicky shows Mike and Paul a [safety needle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_syringe "Safety syringe"), invented by her family friend, Jeffrey Dancort, which defends against accidental [needlesticks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needlestick_injury "Needlestick injury") by only being used once, and she urges them to help bring the product to hospitals. Vicky later dies from her illness. Mike digs deeper into the case, and discovers no one is willing to buy the needle because of a healthcare/pharmaceutical conspiracy and bribery racket. With the threat of exposure, heavyweight attorneys move in on the defense led by attorney Nathaniel Price. Out of their league and out of money, the mounting pressure of the case pushes the two underdog lawyers and their business to the breaking point.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

In the meantime, Mike is struggling with his heavy drug usage and his loneliness. He seeks sex therapy as a source of comfort and is consistently in the company of prostitutes. His personal struggles hinder the realization of his professional ambitions, as he misses many of the meetings and investment events, driving a wedge between him and Paul.

Mike, Paul, and Dancort gain the support of Senator O'Reilly, not before she gives Mike an ultimatum: get clean. Mike's heavy withdrawal leaves him hospitalized, only adding to the financial burdens of the firm. The momentum of the case seems to come to a standstill: Senator O'Reilly pulls out after United Medical Health Supplies lobbies for her re-election campaign and Paul, with a new baby at home, is not interested in pursuing the case over his family.

They meet with Nathaniel Price, and he offers a settlement, the tipping point for the conflict between Mike and Paul. Their conflict comes to a head as Mike argues to take the case to trial and seek justice, while Paul protests there is no feasible way they can continue all the way financially. Mike meets a former employee of Thompson Needle Manufacturers and a friend of Vicky's, who implores him to continue the case on behalf of the lives affected by used needles, which spread AIDS and [hepatitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepatitis "Hepatitis") worldwide. Mike meets with Nathaniel Price and pledges he will personally find new clients and hospital employees affected by these unsafe needles across the country. However, the next day, Paul finds Mike dead from an overdose.

At the settlement conference, Paul walks in with famous personal injury attorney [Mark Lanier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Lanier "Mark Lanier"), declining the settlement and proclaiming that they will see them in court. The movie's postscript tells the audience that in 2004, Attorney Lanier settled a lawsuit against one of the nation's largest medical supply manufacturers for over $150 million.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) "As a result, thousands of hospitals throughout the United States now use [safety needles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_syringe "Safety syringe")."

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Puncture_\(film\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

The original story was written by Danziger. Filming began on February 10, 2010, in [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) The film was directed by [Adam Kassen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Kassen "Adam Kassen") and [Mark Kassen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Kassen "Mark Kassen"). Adam Kassen was quoted as saying, "From the moment we heard about this story, we connected to what it says about the current state of our medical industry and the flawed hero that tries to fix it."[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) The director dedicated the film to the real life attorney [Michael David Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_David_Weiss "Michael David Weiss") who died in 1999 of a drug overdose at age 32\.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Puncture_\(film\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Release")\]

After the film premiered at the 2011 [Tribeca Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribeca_Film_Festival "Tribeca Film Festival"), Millennium Films acquired the distribution rights.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) It had a limited release on September 23, 2011, and played in five theaters. The total domestic gross was $68,945.[\[1\]](#cite_note-mojo-1)

*Puncture* was released on DVD and Blu-ray on January 3, 2012\.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) The film promotes safe needle use worldwide.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10)

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Puncture_\(film\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Reception")\]

[Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), a [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator"), reports that 51% of 41 surveyed critics gave the film a positive review, and the average rating was 5\.6/10; the site consensus reads: "There's a compelling story at the heart of *Puncture* but viewers will have to pierce through the formulaic storytelling to find it."[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic") rated it 54/100 based on 17 reviews.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12)

[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") rated it 3/4 stars and wrote that Evans' performance upstages the issues raised in the film.[\[13\]](#cite_note-:0-13) On Evans' performance, Ebert writes, "Electrifying in the role, Evans reminds me of other great out-of-control druggies played by Al Pacino and Nicolas Cage. A movie like this is a reminder that box-office success can be unfair and limiting to gifted young actors."[\[13\]](#cite_note-:0-13)

Kirk Honeycutt of *[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")* wrote, "The film is chock-a-block with extraordinary performances and no one will fault the filmmaking either. This is a well-made movie, make no mistake. It just suffers from a dysfunctional hero."[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) Ronnie Scheib of *[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")* wrote, "Though conceptually intriguing, the mix of downward drug spiral with uphill struggle for good never really coalesces."[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) Jeannette Catsoulis of *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* wrote, "Notable at least in part for its fumbled potential, this health-care-industry melodrama possesses all the right ingredients: an idealistic young lawyer, a corrupt corporate villain and a sympathetic victim. It just fails to assemble them into a compelling whole."[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

2011 American film

Puncture

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/ae/Puncture_Poster.jpg/250px-Puncture_Poster.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Puncture_Poster.jpg) Theatrical release poster

Directed by | [Adam Kassen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Kassen "Adam Kassen") [Mark Kassen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Kassen "Mark Kassen")

Written by | Chris Lopata

Story by | Ela Thier Paul Danziger

Produced by | Adam Kassen Mark Kassen [Jordan Foley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_Foley "Jordan Foley")

Starring | [Chris Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Evans_\(actor\) "Chris Evans (actor)") Mark Kassen [Vinessa Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinessa_Shaw "Vinessa Shaw") [Brett Cullen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Cullen "Brett Cullen") [Michael Biehn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Biehn "Michael Biehn") [Marshall Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Bell "Marshall Bell")

Cinematography | Helge Gerull

Edited by | Chip Smith

Music by | Ryan Ross Smith

Production company | [Millennium Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alchemy_\(company\) "Alchemy (company)")

Distributed by | Millennium Entertainment

Release date | - April 21, 2011 (2011-04-21) (Tribeca)

Running time | 99 minutes

Country | United States

Language | English

Box office | $123,700[\[1\]](#cite_note-mojo-1)

***Puncture*** (released under the title ***Injustice*** in the United Kingdom) is an independent feature film starring [Chris Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Evans_\(actor\) "Chris Evans (actor)"), directed by [Adam Kassen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Kassen "Adam Kassen") and [Mark Kassen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Kassen "Mark Kassen"). The film is based on the true story of [Michael David "Mike" Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_David_Weiss "Michael David Weiss") and Paul Danziger. It was chosen as one of the spotlight films for the 2011 [Tribeca Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribeca_Film_Festival "Tribeca Film Festival"), premiering on April 21, 2011, in New York City.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Puncture_\(film\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

Mike Weiss, a young Houston lawyer and drug addict, and Paul Danziger, his longtime friend and straitlaced law partner, are the personal injury lawyers behind the law firm Danziger & Weiss. They decide to take on a case involving Vicky Rogers, a local ER nurse, who was [pricked by a contaminated needle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needlestick_injury "Needlestick injury") on the job and contracted HIV. Vicky shows Mike and Paul a [safety needle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_syringe "Safety syringe"), invented by her family friend, Jeffrey Dancort, which defends against accidental [needlesticks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needlestick_injury "Needlestick injury") by only being used once, and she urges them to help bring the product to hospitals. Vicky later dies from her illness. Mike digs deeper into the case, and discovers no one is willing to buy the needle because of a healthcare/pharmaceutical conspiracy and bribery racket. With the threat of exposure, heavyweight attorneys move in on the defense led by attorney Nathaniel Price. Out of their league and out of money, the mounting pressure of the case pushes the two underdog lawyers and their business to the breaking point.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

In the meantime, Mike is struggling with his heavy drug usage and his loneliness. He seeks sex therapy as a source of comfort and is consistently in the company of prostitutes. His personal struggles hinder the realization of his professional ambitions, as he misses many of the meetings and investment events, driving a wedge between him and Paul.

Mike, Paul, and Dancort gain the support of Senator O'Reilly, not before she gives Mike an ultimatum: get clean. Mike's heavy withdrawal leaves him hospitalized, only adding to the financial burdens of the firm. The momentum of the case seems to come to a standstill: Senator O'Reilly pulls out after United Medical Health Supplies lobbies for her re-election campaign and Paul, with a new baby at home, is not interested in pursuing the case over his family.

They meet with Nathaniel Price, and he offers a settlement, the tipping point for the conflict between Mike and Paul. Their conflict comes to a head as Mike argues to take the case to trial and seek justice, while Paul protests there is no feasible way they can continue all the way financially. Mike meets a former employee of Thompson Needle Manufacturers and a friend of Vicky's, who implores him to continue the case on behalf of the lives affected by used needles, which spread AIDS and [hepatitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepatitis "Hepatitis") worldwide. Mike meets with Nathaniel Price and pledges he will personally find new clients and hospital employees affected by these unsafe needles across the country. However, the next day, Paul finds Mike dead from an overdose.

At the settlement conference, Paul walks in with famous personal injury attorney [Mark Lanier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Lanier "Mark Lanier"), declining the settlement and proclaiming that they will see them in court. The movie's postscript tells the audience that in 2004, Attorney Lanier settled a lawsuit against one of the nation's largest medical supply manufacturers for over $150 million.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) "As a result, thousands of hospitals throughout the United States now use [safety needles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_syringe "Safety syringe")."

- [Chris Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Evans_\(actor\) "Chris Evans (actor)") as Atty. [Michael David 'Mike' Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_David_Weiss "Michael David Weiss") \- Drug addict partner

- [Brett Cullen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Cullen "Brett Cullen") as Nathaniel Price \- Attorney for United Medical group

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Puncture_\(film\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

The original story was written by Danziger. Filming began on February 10, 2010, in [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) The film was directed by [Adam Kassen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Kassen "Adam Kassen") and [Mark Kassen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Kassen "Mark Kassen"). Adam Kassen was quoted as saying, "From the moment we heard about this story, we connected to what it says about the current state of our medical industry and the flawed hero that tries to fix it."[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) The director dedicated the film to the real life attorney [Michael David Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_David_Weiss "Michael David Weiss") who died in 1999 of a drug overdose at age 32\.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Puncture_\(film\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Release")\]

After the film premiered at the 2011 [Tribeca Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribeca_Film_Festival "Tribeca Film Festival"), Millennium Films acquired the distribution rights.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) It had a limited release on September 23, 2011, and played in five theaters. The total domestic gross was $68,945.[\[1\]](#cite_note-mojo-1)

*Puncture* was released on DVD and Blu-ray on January 3, 2012\.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) The film promotes safe needle use worldwide.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10)

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Puncture_\(film\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Reception")\]

[Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), a [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator"), reports that 51% of 41 surveyed critics gave the film a positive review, and the average rating was 5\.6/10; the site consensus reads: "There's a compelling story at the heart of *Puncture* but viewers will have to pierce through the formulaic storytelling to find it."[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic") rated it 54/100 based on 17 reviews.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12)

[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") rated it 3/4 stars and wrote that Evans' performance upstages the issues raised in the film.[\[13\]](#cite_note-:0-13) On Evans' performance, Ebert writes, "Electrifying in the role, Evans reminds me of other great out-of-control druggies played by Al Pacino and Nicolas Cage. A movie like this is a reminder that box-office success can be unfair and limiting to gifted young actors."[\[13\]](#cite_note-:0-13)

Kirk Honeycutt of *[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")* wrote, "The film is chock-a-block with extraordinary performances and no one will fault the filmmaking either. This is a well-made movie, make no mistake. It just suffers from a dysfunctional hero."[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) Ronnie Scheib of *[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")* wrote, "Though conceptually intriguing, the mix of downward drug spiral with uphill struggle for good never really coalesces."[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) Jeannette Catsoulis of *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* wrote, "Notable at least in part for its fumbled potential, this health-care-industry melodrama possesses all the right ingredients: an idealistic young lawyer, a corrupt corporate villain and a sympathetic victim. It just fails to assemble them into a compelling whole."[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

***The Boys from Brazil*** is a 1978 British-American [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") [thriller film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thriller_film "Thriller film") directed by [Franklin J. Schaffner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_J._Schaffner "Franklin J. Schaffner"). It stars [Gregory Peck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_Peck "Gregory Peck") and [Laurence Olivier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier "Laurence Olivier"), and features [James Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Mason "James Mason"), [Lilli Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilli_Palmer "Lilli Palmer"), [Uta Hagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uta_Hagen "Uta Hagen"), [Rosemary Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosemary_Harris "Rosemary Harris"), [Anne Meara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Meara "Anne Meara"), [Denholm Elliott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denholm_Elliott "Denholm Elliott"), and [Steve Guttenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Guttenberg "Steve Guttenberg") in supporting roles. The film is based on the [1976 novel of the same title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(novel\) "The Boys from Brazil (novel)") by [Ira Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ira_Levin "Ira Levin"). It was nominated for three [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards").

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

Barry Kohler, a young amateur [Nazi hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_hunter "Nazi hunter"), spies on a meeting of the fugitive Nazi organization *[Kameraden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ODESSA "ODESSA")* in [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay"). At this meeting, infamous [Auschwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auschwitz_concentration_camp "Auschwitz concentration camp") doctor [Josef Mengele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Mengele "Josef Mengele") provides instructions for the assassinations of 94 [civil servants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_servant "Civil servant") in Western Europe and North America, all of them low-ranking and aged around 65, on particular dates over the next two years. Kohler telephones Ezra Lieberman, a famous (as well as penniless and cynical) Nazi hunter living in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), to inform him of his discovery. While still on the phone, Kohler is discovered by the *Kameraden* and killed.

With the help of his sister Esther, British journalist Sidney Beynon and [Jewish-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish-American "Jewish-American") [vigilante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigilante "Vigilante") leader David Bennett, Lieberman begins investigating the deaths of civil servants fitting the profile who die suddenly over the next several months. He is struck by the fact that all of the dead men have sons aged 13 who look exactly alike, with pale skin, dark hair and blue eyes. He discovers that all of the boys were [illegally adopted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adoption_fraud "Adoption fraud") and that some of the adoptions were facilitated by *Kameraden* member Frieda Maloney, who has since been imprisoned. Lieberman interviews Maloney, who tells him that the boys were provided by an intermediary in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"). She mentions that one of the adoptive fathers she dealt with, American Henry Wheelock, gave her a newborn puppy in exchange for her baby.

Seeking an explanation for the boys' identical appearance, Lieberman consults the biologist Dr. Bruckner, who explains the principles of [cloning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloning "Cloning"). Lieberman deduces that the boys are clones of [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler"), all created from a single [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") sample by Mengele, who has also been seeking to ensure that their childhoods imitate that of the original Hitler by having them adopted by parents who resemble Hitler's own abusive father [Alois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alois_Hitler "Alois Hitler") (a civil servant in the [Austro-Hungarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Empire "Austro-Hungarian Empire")) and doting mother [Klara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klara_Hitler "Klara Hitler"). This is done in the hopes that their later lives will follow the same course, and that as adults they will establish [new Nazi regimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Nazism "Neo-Nazism") in their respective countries. The murders of the fathers are part of this plan, designed to reflect the death of Alois when Hitler was 13\. Based on this revelation, and the age of Maloney's dog, Lieberman understands that Henry Wheelock is due to be murdered in just four days' time.

Alarmed by the progress of Lieberman's investigation and Mengele's increasingly erratic behavior (after he almost dispatches one of his men for killing his target on the wrong date), the *Kameraden* leadership attempts to shut down the project, but Mengele escapes and his laboratory gets destroyed by Eduard Sibert, a retired German colonel.

Lieberman travels to rural [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") to warn Wheelock of the patricide, only to discover that Wheelock has already been murdered by Mengele, impersonating Lieberman. In the proceeding struggle, Mengele severely wounds Lieberman, but is then cornered by the family's vicious [Doberman Pinschers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doberman_Pinscher "Doberman Pinscher") (Mengele fears dogs). When Wheelock's son Bobby arrives home from school, Mengele attempts to tell him about his real origins. He does not make any attempts to deny killing Wheelock, telling Bobby that he must rise above his worthless adoptive family and embrace his destiny. This enrages Bobby, who orders the dogs to kill Mengele. Lieberman recovers a list from Mengele's pocket detailing the identities of all 94 clones, and then collapses from blood loss.

As Lieberman recuperates in hospital, he is visited by Bennett who asks him to hand over the list so that his vigilante group can eliminate the clones. Lieberman refuses and instead burns the list, declaring that they are innocent children who may yet grow up to be harmless. The final scene shows Bobby gazing in fascination at photographs he took of Mengele's mauled corpse.

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

### Development

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")\]

The book came out in 1976 and was a best seller.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) In August 1976 it was announced the Producers Group (Robert Fryer, Martin Richards, Mary Lee Johnson and James Cresson) had optioned the film rights to the novel and would make the movie in association with [Lew Grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lew_Grade "Lew Grade").[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) Fryer had just made *Voyage of the Damned* for Grade.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) According to producer [Martin Richards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Richards_\(producer\) "Martin Richards (producer)"), [Robert Mulligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mulligan "Robert Mulligan") was the original director.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)

In May 1977, it was announced [Laurence Olivier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier "Laurence Olivier") would star.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) By this stage Franklin Schaffner was attached to direct.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) Gregory Peck joined the film in July.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) Olivier had recently been ill and was taking as many well-paying movie jobs as he could get in order to provide for his wife and children after his death.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) Peck agreed to portray Mengele only because he wanted to work with Olivier.[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) Mason initially expressed interest in playing either Mengele or Lieberman.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) Lilli Palmer also accepted a small role just to work with Olivier.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) To prepare for the roles of the European clones, Jeremy Black was sent to a speech studio in New York City by 20th Century Fox to learn how to speak with both an English and a German accent.[\[16\]](#cite_note-black-16)

"The emphasis of the film is not on Nazis," said producer Fryer. "It is really about cloning, a logical extension of existing facts. And it's about the hatred that two men have for each other."[\[17\]](#cite_note-clip-17)

### Filming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Filming")\]

Although the bulk of the film is set in South America, Fryer says actually filming on that continent was "logistically impossible" so the decision was made to shoot it in Lisbon, Portugal.[\[17\]](#cite_note-clip-17) Filming started in Portugal in October 1977, with additional filming in London, Vienna, the [Kölnbrein Dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kölnbrein_Dam "Kölnbrein Dam") in Austria, and Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The scenes that were set in Massachusetts were shot in London.[\[16\]](#cite_note-black-16)[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)

The altercation between Lieberman and Mengele took about three or four days to film due to Olivier's ailing health at the time. Peck recalled that he and Olivier "were lying around on the floor" laughing at the absurdity of having to film such a fight scene at their advanced ages.[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)

### Extended ending

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Extended ending")\]

A brief end segment with Bobby Wheelock in a darkroom was restored to some versions in later years. In this alternative ending, after Lieberman burns the list in his hospital bed, the scene transitions to Bobby in a darkroom developing photographs of Lieberman and Mengele, with a piercing glare coming from his steely-blue eyes as he focuses on Mengele's jaguar claw bracelet before fading to the end credits.

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Release")\]

The film had 25 minutes cut when released in West Germany, theatrical as well as all subsequent TV, video and some DVD releases. In 1999, by [Artisan Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artisan_Entertainment "Artisan Entertainment"), and 2009 by [Lionsgate Home Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionsgate_Home_Entertainment "Lionsgate Home Entertainment"), the film was released uncut on DVD in the U.S. and uncut in Germany on its DVDs.

[Lew Grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lew_Grade "Lew Grade"), who partly financed the film, was not happy with the final result, feeling that the ending was too gory. He says he protested but Franklin J. Schaffner, who had final cut rights, overruled him.[\[20\]](#cite_note-grade-20)

In 2015, [Shout! Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shout!_Factory "Shout! Factory") released the film on Blu-ray.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21)

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Reception")\]

### Critical response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Critical response")\]

On [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film has an approval rating of 72% based on 32 reviews, with an average rating of 6\.3/10. The site's consensus states: "Its story takes some dubious turns, but a high-calibre cast and a gripping pace fashion *The Boys from Brazil* into an effective thriller."[\[22\]](#cite_note-22) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), the film has a score of 40 out of 100 based on reviews from 7 critics, indicating "mixed or average reviews.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23)

*[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")* wrote "With two excellent antagonists in Gregory Peck and Lord Laurence Olivier, *The Boys from Brazil* presents a gripping, suspenseful drama for nearly all of its two hours — then lets go at the end and falls into a heap."[\[24\]](#cite_note-24) [Gene Siskel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Siskel "Gene Siskel") of the *[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")* gave the film one-and-a-half out of four stars and called it "old-fashioned filmmaking at its worst," with "one of the phoniest stories you can imagine."[\[25\]](#cite_note-Siskel-25) [Charles Champlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Champlin "Charles Champlin") of the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* wrote "It is penny-dreadful stuff, sumptuously executed but still as shallow as a Saturday serial. One exasperation of *The Boys From Brazil* is that, even accepting the biological possibility of the premise, the script by Heywood Gould never confronts any of the interesting questions raised."[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) Gary Arnold of *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")* called it "admirably crafted and surprisingly effective," and "a snazzy pop entertainment synthesis of accumulating suspense, detective work, pseudoscientific speculation and historical wish fulfillment."[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) [Pauline Kael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Kael "Pauline Kael") of *[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker "The New Yorker")* wrote "If the film wants to be taken as a cautionary fable—another one!—about the ever-present dangers of Nazism, then it should leave viewers with a sense of menace that Mengele's 'boys from Brazil' constitute. Instead, we get Lieberman's fuddy-duddy humanism and vague assurances that the boys are not really dangerous. And this is supposed to be a movie."[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) [Jack Kroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kroll "Jack Kroll") of *[Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek "Newsweek")* wrote that "the thoughts aren't quite deep enough even for a thriller...Heywood Gould's reasonably suspenseful screenplay blows it by suddenly turning Lieberman into a kindly old Jewish uncle instead of a man who is willing to face the tough paradoxes of good and evil."[\[29\]](#cite_note-29)

Scholars have used the film's idea of controlling an individual's genetics and upbringing to illustrate the difficulties of reconciling traditional views of free will with modern neuroscience.[\[30\]](#cite_note-30)

***The Boys from Brazil*** is a 1978 British-American [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") [thriller film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thriller_film "Thriller film") directed by [Franklin J. Schaffner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_J._Schaffner "Franklin J. Schaffner"). It stars [Gregory Peck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_Peck "Gregory Peck") and [Laurence Olivier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier "Laurence Olivier"), and features [James Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Mason "James Mason"), [Lilli Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilli_Palmer "Lilli Palmer"), [Uta Hagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uta_Hagen "Uta Hagen"), [Rosemary Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosemary_Harris "Rosemary Harris"), [Anne Meara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Meara "Anne Meara"), [Denholm Elliott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denholm_Elliott "Denholm Elliott"), and [Steve Guttenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Guttenberg "Steve Guttenberg") in supporting roles. The film is based on the [1976 novel of the same title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(novel\) "The Boys from Brazil (novel)") by [Ira Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ira_Levin "Ira Levin"). It was nominated for three [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards").

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

Barry Kohler, a young amateur [Nazi hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_hunter "Nazi hunter"), spies on a meeting of the fugitive Nazi organization *[Kameraden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ODESSA "ODESSA")* in [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay"). At this meeting, infamous [Auschwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auschwitz_concentration_camp "Auschwitz concentration camp") doctor [Josef Mengele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Mengele "Josef Mengele") provides instructions for the assassinations of 94 [civil servants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_servant "Civil servant") in Western Europe and North America, all of them low-ranking and aged around 65, on particular dates over the next two years. Kohler telephones Ezra Lieberman, a famous (as well as penniless and cynical) Nazi hunter living in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), to inform him of his discovery. While still on the phone, Kohler is discovered by the *Kameraden* and killed.

With the help of his sister Esther, British journalist Sidney Beynon and [Jewish-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish-American "Jewish-American") [vigilante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigilante "Vigilante") leader David Bennett, Lieberman begins investigating the deaths of civil servants fitting the profile who die suddenly over the next several months. He is struck by the fact that all of the dead men have sons aged 13 who look exactly alike, with pale skin, dark hair and blue eyes. He discovers that all of the boys were [illegally adopted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adoption_fraud "Adoption fraud") and that some of the adoptions were facilitated by *Kameraden* member Frieda Maloney, who has since been imprisoned. Lieberman interviews Maloney, who tells him that the boys were provided by an intermediary in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"). She mentions that one of the adoptive fathers she dealt with, American Henry Wheelock, gave her a newborn puppy in exchange for her baby.

Seeking an explanation for the boys' identical appearance, Lieberman consults the biologist Dr. Bruckner, who explains the principles of [cloning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloning "Cloning"). Lieberman deduces that the boys are clones of [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler"), all created from a single [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") sample by Mengele, who has also been seeking to ensure that their childhoods imitate that of the original Hitler by having them adopted by parents who resemble Hitler's own abusive father [Alois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alois_Hitler "Alois Hitler") (a civil servant in the [Austro-Hungarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Empire "Austro-Hungarian Empire")) and doting mother [Klara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klara_Hitler "Klara Hitler"). This is done in the hopes that their later lives will follow the same course, and that as adults they will establish [new Nazi regimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Nazism "Neo-Nazism") in their respective countries. The murders of the fathers are part of this plan, designed to reflect the death of Alois when Hitler was 13\. Based on this revelation, and the age of Maloney's dog, Lieberman understands that Henry Wheelock is due to be murdered in just four days' time.

Alarmed by the progress of Lieberman's investigation and Mengele's increasingly erratic behavior (after he almost dispatches one of his men for killing his target on the wrong date), the *Kameraden* leadership attempts to shut down the project, but Mengele escapes and his laboratory gets destroyed by Eduard Sibert, a retired German colonel.

Lieberman travels to rural [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") to warn Wheelock of the patricide, only to discover that Wheelock has already been murdered by Mengele, impersonating Lieberman. In the proceeding struggle, Mengele severely wounds Lieberman, but is then cornered by the family's vicious [Doberman Pinschers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doberman_Pinscher "Doberman Pinscher") (Mengele fears dogs). When Wheelock's son Bobby arrives home from school, Mengele attempts to tell him about his real origins. He does not make any attempts to deny killing Wheelock, telling Bobby that he must rise above his worthless adoptive family and embrace his destiny. This enrages Bobby, who orders the dogs to kill Mengele. Lieberman recovers a list from Mengele's pocket detailing the identities of all 94 clones, and then collapses from blood loss.

As Lieberman recuperates in hospital, he is visited by Bennett who asks him to hand over the list so that his vigilante group can eliminate the clones. Lieberman refuses and instead burns the list, declaring that they are innocent children who may yet grow up to be harmless. The final scene shows Bobby gazing in fascination at photographs he took of Mengele's mauled corpse.

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

### Development

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")\]

The book came out in 1976 and was a best seller.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) In August 1976 it was announced the Producers Group (Robert Fryer, Martin Richards, Mary Lee Johnson and James Cresson) had optioned the film rights to the novel and would make the movie in association with [Lew Grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lew_Grade "Lew Grade").[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) Fryer had just made *Voyage of the Damned* for Grade.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) According to producer [Martin Richards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Richards_\(producer\) "Martin Richards (producer)"), [Robert Mulligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mulligan "Robert Mulligan") was the original director.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)

In May 1977, it was announced [Laurence Olivier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier "Laurence Olivier") would star.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) By this stage Franklin Schaffner was attached to direct.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) Gregory Peck joined the film in July.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) Olivier had recently been ill and was taking as many well-paying movie jobs as he could get in order to provide for his wife and children after his death.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) Peck agreed to portray Mengele only because he wanted to work with Olivier.[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) Mason initially expressed interest in playing either Mengele or Lieberman.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) Lilli Palmer also accepted a small role just to work with Olivier.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) To prepare for the roles of the European clones, Jeremy Black was sent to a speech studio in New York City by 20th Century Fox to learn how to speak with both an English and a German accent.[\[16\]](#cite_note-black-16)

"The emphasis of the film is not on Nazis," said producer Fryer. "It is really about cloning, a logical extension of existing facts. And it's about the hatred that two men have for each other."[\[17\]](#cite_note-clip-17)

### Filming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Filming")\]

Although the bulk of the film is set in South America, Fryer says actually filming on that continent was "logistically impossible" so the decision was made to shoot it in Lisbon, Portugal.[\[17\]](#cite_note-clip-17) Filming started in Portugal in October 1977, with additional filming in London, Vienna, the [Kölnbrein Dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kölnbrein_Dam "Kölnbrein Dam") in Austria, and Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The scenes that were set in Massachusetts were shot in London.[\[16\]](#cite_note-black-16)[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)

The altercation between Lieberman and Mengele took about three or four days to film due to Olivier's ailing health at the time. Peck recalled that he and Olivier "were lying around on the floor" laughing at the absurdity of having to film such a fight scene at their advanced ages.[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)

### Extended ending

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Extended ending")\]

A brief end segment with Bobby Wheelock in a darkroom was restored to some versions in later years. In this alternative ending, after Lieberman burns the list in his hospital bed, the scene transitions to Bobby in a darkroom developing photographs of Lieberman and Mengele, with a piercing glare coming from his steely-blue eyes as he focuses on Mengele's jaguar claw bracelet before fading to the end credits.

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Release")\]

The film had 25 minutes cut when released in West Germany, theatrical as well as all subsequent TV, video and some DVD releases. In 1999, by [Artisan Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artisan_Entertainment "Artisan Entertainment"), and 2009 by [Lionsgate Home Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionsgate_Home_Entertainment "Lionsgate Home Entertainment"), the film was released uncut on DVD in the U.S. and uncut in Germany on its DVDs.

[Lew Grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lew_Grade "Lew Grade"), who partly financed the film, was not happy with the final result, feeling that the ending was too gory. He says he protested but Franklin J. Schaffner, who had final cut rights, overruled him.[\[20\]](#cite_note-grade-20)

In 2015, [Shout! Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shout!_Factory "Shout! Factory") released the film on Blu-ray.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21)

## Reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Reception")\]

### Critical response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Boys_from_Brazil_\(film\)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Critical response")\]

On [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film has an approval rating of 72% based on 32 reviews, with an average rating of 6\.3/10. The site's consensus states: "Its story takes some dubious turns, but a high-calibre cast and a gripping pace fashion *The Boys from Brazil* into an effective thriller."[\[22\]](#cite_note-22) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), the film has a score of 40 out of 100 based on reviews from 7 critics, indicating "mixed or average reviews.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23)

*[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")* wrote "With two excellent antagonists in Gregory Peck and Lord Laurence Olivier, *The Boys from Brazil* presents a gripping, suspenseful drama for nearly all of its two hours — then lets go at the end and falls into a heap."[\[24\]](#cite_note-24) [Gene Siskel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Siskel "Gene Siskel") of the *[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")* gave the film one-and-a-half out of four stars and called it "old-fashioned filmmaking at its worst," with "one of the phoniest stories you can imagine."[\[25\]](#cite_note-Siskel-25) [Charles Champlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Champlin "Charles Champlin") of the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* wrote "It is penny-dreadful stuff, sumptuously executed but still as shallow as a Saturday serial. One exasperation of *The Boys From Brazil* is that, even accepting the biological possibility of the premise, the script by Heywood Gould never confronts any of the interesting questions raised."[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) Gary Arnold of *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")* called it "admirably crafted and surprisingly effective," and "a snazzy pop entertainment synthesis of accumulating suspense, detective work, pseudoscientific speculation and historical wish fulfillment."[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) [Pauline Kael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Kael "Pauline Kael") of *[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker "The New Yorker")* wrote "If the film wants to be taken as a cautionary fable—another one!—about the ever-present dangers of Nazism, then it should leave viewers with a sense of menace that Mengele's 'boys from Brazil' constitute. Instead, we get Lieberman's fuddy-duddy humanism and vague assurances that the boys are not really dangerous. And this is supposed to be a movie."[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) [Jack Kroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kroll "Jack Kroll") of *[Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek "Newsweek")* wrote that "the thoughts aren't quite deep enough even for a thriller...Heywood Gould's reasonably suspenseful screenplay blows it by suddenly turning Lieberman into a kindly old Jewish uncle instead of a man who is willing to face the tough paradoxes of good and evil."[\[29\]](#cite_note-29)

Scholars have used the film's idea of controlling an individual's genetics and upbringing to illustrate the difficulties of reconciling traditional views of free will with modern neuroscience.[\[30\]](#cite_note-30)
